speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to take this opportunity to say on behalf of those of us on this side of the house that we agree with the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Harkness) that this is no time for pacificism or neutralism. The Canadian temperament is neither. It has not been in the past, and is not now.
Several times Canadians have been called upon to take up arms in the name of freedom, and each time, without hesitation, they have done so willingly and both on this continent and abroad have fought gallantly for the things in which they believed.
We cannot be neutralist. To be neutralist is to be nothing. We are for something; we are for freedom. If we are for freedom we cannot be neutralist in this struggle. It is not enough to have freedom in Canada. We have to covet this belief for all peoples everywhere.
Mr. Khrushchev said, when visiting this continent, that he intends to bury us. Surely we have to take him at his word. Surely he means what he says, and even if he does not mean that he will bury us by means of force of arms, he means that he will attempt to do so by some other means, whether by the use of economic pressure or through an intensification of the ideological warfare which has been taking place now for some years.
We have to take this threat seriously and we have to do something about it. We are involved in an all-out struggle between two forms of government, the totalitarian on one side and the libertarian on the other. How, in this circumstance, can we be neutral? It is a struggle between tyranny and freedom.
Many people in this country know from bitter experience what freedom really means. Included in the more than one million postwar immigrants who have come to this country are a great many political refugees who have come from various countries behind the iron curtain. Some of them have been

personally persecuted because of their belief in freedom. Some of them have had families persecuted. Some of them have lost their families. Some of them have spent terms in prison camps in Siberia because they refused to be cowed by political tyranny. Believe me, they know what the word "freedom" means, and they are the vanguard of trying to keep this country stirred up to the point where we will not shirk our responsibility.
They know the meaning of freedom. The people from the Baltic states know the meaning of freedom; the people who have come here from Poland or Hungary, or any of the other countries behind the iron curtain, know that there is in fact a struggle and it is going to be waged until one side emerges victorious, either those who believe in the totalitarian system of government or those who believe, as most of us do, in freedom for all peoples to choose for themselves the way in which they would like to live. There can be no neutralism amongst them, and indeed they set a standard for us.
In this situation we must stand with our United States friends. True enough, they do things from time to time which annoy us. True enough from time to time they take us for granted. But notwithstanding that, when all the froth is swept away we must stand beside them, because they are carrying the burden of freedom in the western world and will continue to do so. The least we can do is to make sure that we co-operate with them in any useful venture which will strengthen the western world in this all-out struggle.
Coming now to the means of co-operation, may I say that this government has contributed considerably to the present tendency among some very small minority groups in this country toward pacifism and neutralism.

It is because of people such as these to whom I have referred-we may not agree with all they say but they are good Canadian citizens putting forth their views- that we in this group think it is most unfortunate, most improper, out of line with our Canadian tradition, that the hon. member and gallant Minister of National Defence (Mr. Harkness)-and I give him full credit in that direction; I know of his record in war- should suggest to the officers of the reserve forces that they should go out and use their influence to defeat the efforts of the very women who have received the blessing of the Prime Minister, the Secretary of State for External Affairs, the Leader of the Opposition, the leader of the hon. member for Trinity, and the national leader of the C.C.F. I protest very strongly. This may seem to be a minor matter, but it is a precedent, it is the first time. I do urge on behalf of this group that the minister give this question very serious consideration. We trust, Mr. Speaker, that after listening to the remarks of the members on the opposition side of the house and having a quiet night of sleep and meditation, he will return in the very near future and correct his unfortunate position in this respect.

speakeroldname: Hon. D. S. Harkness (Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the members to your immediate left, the C.C.F. party, have been very well known in the past for their ability to attempt to make mountains out of molehills. I think they have surpassed themselves tonight; they have tried to make a mountain range out of a grain of sand. The hon. member for Bumaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Regier) has made various accusations against me based on the story written by a reporter who was not present at the time that the alleged remarks were supposed to have been made and which, as I indicated this afternoon, did not bear a very close resemblance to what I actually said at the mess dinner in question.
A great deal of this talk that we have had from the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquit-lam and the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) seemed to revolve around nuclear weapons and so on. As I made it extremely clear this afternoon, I made absolutely no mention of nuclear weapons at this particular mess dinner. I did not have them in mind in any way whatever and I think anybody who was present at the mess dinner would be prepared to say that that is so, that there was no mention of them whatever.
Then, of course, the hon. member went on and attempted to state or to give the impression that this is what I was talking about; that then I was attempting in some way to

National Defence
introduce politics and to make political converts, or something else along that line, at the mess dinner. Nothing was further from my mind and nothing, I am absolutely sure, was further from the mind of any member of H.M.C.S. Carleton who was present. The effort, supposition, imagination or whatever you should like to call it on the part of hon. members opposite who tried to make out that there was anything political in the remarks that I made is completely absurd. There was nothing political in them whatever. There was no attempt made and no idea of there being anything political in them, and if my hon. friends in the Liberal party would like to ask the son of one of their senators who was there I think he will completely confirm that that was the situation. Certainly nobody ever raised any such idea or had any idea along that line as far as I am aware, and I am quite sure that this is so because there was no excuse for it at this particular dinner.
I hope this effectively disposes of the two allegations which have been made by hon. members opposite in connection with the remarks I made at this particular mess dinner.
The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam tried to make a point of the fact that there was a copy of the speech, and then there was none, and so on. Then he said there was something that had been issued by an officer of H.M.C.S. Carleton. I can assure the hon. member and all other hon. members that I went to this mess dinner without any pieces of paper of any kind, and I spoke entirely off the cuff without any notes such as those in my hand, or of any nature whatever and, therefore, naturally there was no copy of the speech.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: The minister admitted it earlier today.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: He did not.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: I did not admit any such thing; I could not have admitted any such thing because there was no such copy in existence, as a matter of fact. This is just another example of how the hon. member imagines something and then tries to put words in somebody else's mouth and makes completely incorrect accusations.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Just read Hansard.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
Completely without my
knowledge, apparently one of the officers who was present at this mess dinner, and I presume he has the right to do so if he wishes, did put out some sort of account of what went on at the dinner and this was, I presume, issued to the press. However, as far as I am concerned, as far as my office is concerned, there is absolutely nothing to any accusations

such as the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer) made that there was a modified version issued from my office. I saw this reported in newspaper accounts and I questioned the people in my office. After investigation they came back and told me that this was completely incorrect.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: This came from a very reliable source.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: This is another example of the way in which this matter has been blown up out of all recognition and a certain amount of confusion seems to have arisen over it.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: We could not get anything out of your office.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: I should like to make it clear again that at this mess dinner I expressed my opposition to neutralism and to pacifism as expounded by those who advocate unilateral disarmament and so on as far as Canada is concerned, and I expect to continue voicing my opposition to ideas of that kind. I think I would be a very poor minister of national defence if I did anything else. I quite understand that the C.C.F. party has a neutralist and pacifist outlook-

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: That is boloney and you know it.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: -and policy.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: That is boloney.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Determined at Regina.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
However, I would be very much surprised if any considerable proportion of the Canadian people supports them in that attitude. In fact, I feel quite convinced that the great majority of the Canadian people are just as determined as I am to see that the country's security is properly protected and the country is properly defended.
The hon. member for Trinity, as is usual with the Liberal party with respect to defence matters, was trying to be on both sides of the fence. He applauded the kind of remarks I made but at the same time he tried to say that I should not have made them, that there was a political manoeuvre or something of that sort on my part in making these remarks at this particular mess dinner.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Very logical and consistent.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
Of course, I have already dealt with that point. This is not the time to enter into a debate on defence policy. In fact, Mr. Speaker prevented the hon. member for Trinity from pursuing that line as he was attempting to do, but I must say I was extremely surprised at the general line taken by the hon. member in view of

the resolutions passed at the Liberal rally over which he presided as chairman.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Phony Liberal policies.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, you ruled that this kind of discussion was out of order and the Minister of National Defence, acknowledging that that ruling has been made, now defies it. I suggest to Your Honour with great respect that the minister should be asked either to take his seat or to take another line altogether because he is now transgressing a ruling that you made.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Are you one of the bird watchers, Paul?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: I understood that the minister was dealing with some remarks which had been made by the hon. member for Trinity but it is true that he seemed to go beyond that in referring to certain resolutions which have not heretofore been mentioned.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: They want to forget them.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: I shall allow him to continue with the reminder that he himself has already declared that this is not a defence debate.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I agree with your ruling that this is not a defence debate and, as you indicated, I brought up this matter only because the hon. member for Trinity brought it up and was allowed to continue for a considerable length of time. I think it has always been your custom under those circumstances to allow at least a few words in reply-

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Not at all.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: when statements of this kind are made. However, I will only say further in connection with the matter that if the Liberal party could for once come down on one side or the other on this particular question or any other question I think they would be a great deal better off than they are in the extremely ambiguous and anomalous position in which they find themselves at the present time.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Is the hon. member for Vancouver East rising on a new matter?

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: On the same grievance.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
I do not propose to stop the hon. member but I suggest to him that in order that there may be some systematic procedure during the grievance period hon. members who wish to speak to a grievance should do so before the minister concerned replies. No one rose before the minister but 90205-6-102J

as he does not close the debate the hon. member can proceed on this matter if he wishes to do so.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have listened very carefully to what has just been said by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Harkness) and at the outset I want to say that the minister cannot brush this matter aside as being something of no importance. In his opening remarks he stated that we in this group were endeavouring to make a mountain out of a molehill. All I can say is that if it is not a mountain it is a mighty big molehill. The grievance that has been raised is a most important and serious one. It must be or I would not be on my feet.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: That is the biggest joke of all.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
It is quite obvious from the remarks of the Minister of National Defence that as a tactician in the military sense he agrees with the old statement that the best defence is offence because that is exactly the strategy which he used. The grievance that has been raised has nothing whatsoever to do with what is the defence policy or international policy of the C.C.F. or whether we are or are not neutralist or pacifist in our policies. I am not going into that question, except to say that the minister is absolutely wrong there, because that is not the matter before us.
The matter before us is a most serious one. First of all, as has been pointed out by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Her-ridge), this is what we term a break in tradition with respect to what, according to the press, was said at a meeting addressed by the minister and it is also something which, for a minister, was in exceptionally bad taste. I could not help noting, that in his remarks the Minister of National Defence made some reference to a press report but it must have been noted by all that he did not deny the correctness of the press release issued by the public relations officer of H.M.C.S. Carleton. That press release, which has already been quoted and not denied by the minister, reads in part as follows:
Turning to considerations of defence in Canada* Mr. Harkness pointed out that pacifist and ban the bomb movements are apparently being encouraged by groups wishing to prevent Canada from being able to make an effective defence effort. Their propaganda is being well disseminated in the country and the personnel of reserve units of the forces should make an effort to combat it. Being in much closer touch with the general population in their daily lives than men of the regular forces-

National Defence
As I say, it has not been denied and we say that it is in bad taste, that it should not have been done and that it goes beyond tradition with respect to the relationship between a cabinet minister and any segment of the armed forces.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, would the hon. member identify the document from which he read?

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
Yes, I have read from a press release from H.M.C.S. Carleton, Ottawa.
That phase of our grievance has been discussed already by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Regier) and the hon. member for Kootenay West. I should like to speak on a phase of this grievance which is of the utmost seriousness. I refer to the fact that such a statement can only be taken as the policy, the new thinking of the Minister of National Defence, that organizations of Canadian citizens who want to work for peace are basically subversive. This is the only interpretation that can be placed on these remarks which have not been denied, that some of these people are organized to work for peace and to ban the bomb.
It is essential, Mr. Speaker, that the people of Canada should have an understanding of the position of the minister and, therefore, of the government on the question of banning the bomb and on the question of nuclear weapons, not on whether or not we should have them, but on the question of nuclear weapons themselves. I am going to make this statement as brief as I possibly can.
I had the privilege of being named a parliamentary observer to the United Nations during the first two months of the fifteenth general assembly in New York. During those two months I do not believe I missed a day in the plenary sessions or a day in the No. 1 committee in which matters of this nature were discussed. I believe I heard the representatives of 31 countries speak in that No. 1 committee. I heard the speech which was made by the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Diefenbaker) in the plenary session. I want to say here that I thought it was an excellent presentation. I had the privilege also of sitting immediately behind the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Green) when he made his presentation in the No. 1 committee of the proposals put forward on behalf of Canada.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
Order; if I may interrupt the hon. member, it seems to me he is getting afield again. The alleged grievance relates to the advice given by the minister to members of the armed forces at a dinner. It does not relate to defence policy or to meetings of the United Nations. It has to do with a

meeting of the defence forces at a mess dinner, and it is within that scope that the matter ought to be discussed.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: I am completely within that scope. It is not only the fact that the minister made certain statements that is important, but the statements which he has made are imporant. Among those statements is one which can only be construed as an attack on those people who are organized across Canada for the purpose of achieving peace and one of those purposes is to ban the bomb. Surely I can point out the seriousness of what the minister did and the seriousness of what he said.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: How do you know what he said?

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
He has not denied the P.R.O. report here. He has evaded and dodged, but he has not denied it. He did not deny it when he was approached by other members of the radio, T.V. and press corps. He has not denied it in the House of Commons. I maintain, sir, and I know that you will agree with me, that I have the right to discuss the statement that was made and say that we consider it very serious in relation to the statements I distinctly heard time after time in the United Nations during September, October and November which called for a cessation of nuclear testing, which put forward a policy of non-expansion of nuclear testing and which called for immediate action to get the Geneva committee of ten operating again to achieve complete disarmament. Those are things that were said at the United Nations and which we certainly hoped represented government policy.
If there is to go out in the name of the Minister of National Defence, and not denied, this approach that is reported from H.M.C.S. Carleton, then I say it is a matter of serious import to the people of Canada. They do not know what the policy of this government is, and whether or not it is subversive to go out and advocate the banning of the bomb. What is of even greater importance is the reaction of our friends in the United Nations, and in particular the uncommitted nations. I intend to speak on that particular phase when the opportunity presents itself.
I say that this is not something that can be brushed aside. This is a matter of supreme importance to the Canadian people, not so much the fact that the minister made a speech but what was in the speech. I would not term it a directive because he could not give a directive of this nature, but there was at least a definite inference, an indirect direction, that the reserve officers should use their influence in their daily lives

to oppose these movements for peace in Canada along the lines of the ban the bomb movement.
This is a most serious matter. I maintain it is a breach of a cabinet minister's responsibility and something which can only cause confusion in the public mind and in the international mind, something to be most roundly condemned and most bitterly attacked. The minister should exhibit a greater sense of responsibility when he speaks as a minister, whether in this house or outside of it, because whether he likes it or not he does speak as a cabinet minister. The most important thing is not whether he knew the statement would be reported, but what the views of the minister were. I take this matter so seriously in its national and international implications that I believe, unless the minister tells us here and now that this report which he has ignored so far is completely incorrect and that he did not infer anything like that, there is only one thing for the minister to do and that is the decent thing as would be done in Great Britain, immediately resign his portfolio.

speakeroldname: Mr. Egan Chambers (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
suppose, Mr. Speaker, that the government can take some satisfaction from the fact that the only matter the opposition can find upon which to raise a grievance on the first occasion on which an opportunity is presented is a report of what someone said that someone else said that the minister said at a dinner at which no notes were taken. It seems to me that both this afternoon when this matter was first raised, and this evening, the minister has been most clear in explaining, first of all, what he said and, second, how it came about that the press report was in the form in which it appears. He is the Minister of National Defence. He was speaking to members of the armed forces and he spoke on defence. Upon what else would he speak? He expressed his opinion because he is a man who has the courage to express his opinion on this matter.
However, he has made it clear, and the press release that was read out a few minutes ago makes it clear if it is read carefully, that he advocated no political action on the part of his audience; that he did not oppose those who advocate peace. Surely, no government, no group in the history of this country has a greater record in the search for peace and disarmament than this government.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
Nobody made more promises either.
National Defence

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: This was not a question of promises. This was action in the United Nations, action at Geneva and action right in this House of Commons in giving expression to the policies.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Failure in the United Nations, failure at Geneva and failure in the House of Commons.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: It is a new line that the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer) is taking when he says that Canada was responsible for the failure at Geneva.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: I did not say it was responsible. Just that its success is indicated by the results.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
There is a difference, Mr. Speaker, between being in favour of peace and working for peace through the international media that are provided for that work and advocating unilateral disarmament. There is a difference also, I suggest, between those who honestly and from conviction advocate that point of view and those groups who for their own particular and suspicious purposes may foster these movements. I think a close reading of the press release, if indeed it reflects the words of the minister, will show that distinction was made.
However, we have had here this afternoon two extremely interesting demonstrations, one on the part of the C.C.F. party who are attempting to take unto themselves the mantle of being the only group in this country who are in favour of peace and that on the part of the hon. member for Trinity who has announced the third Liberal defence policy in the period of about a month.
Nowhere, Mr. Speaker, has there been the slightest substantiation in any of the speeches made from across the floor of the house of the allegations that the minister in any way acted improperly or the allegation that he did anything in fact but get to his feet and honestly express his opinions on the defence of this country.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker,-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Is the hon. member for Skeena rising to speak on the same matter?

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: On the same subject matter, Mr. Speaker, yes. I have only two or three brief comments to make, some of them occasioned by the remarks of the hon. member who just took his seat. I point out to him that because we have such an inept, bungling government in the house, that this is not the only subject matter that could be made the point of discussion this evening.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
What about divorce?

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: My hon. friend may be desirous of obtaining one or he may need one, but that is his problem not mine.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: "Honi soit qui mal y pense."

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: There is that nasty innuendo again.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Order. The hon. member precipitated the comment by a personal reference which had nothing to do with the subject under discussion.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
The reason that this matter is raised is the extreme and immediate seriousness of it. It is more than a question of differences of opinion in the cabinet which are quite obvious. It is a question of the very lives of the people of this nation and of other nations. The very lives of children are involved if we are going to embark on a program directed to the end of becoming a nuclear power and if we are going to follow the program advocated by the Liberals when they were in office. I do not know what they are advocating now, really; their policy moves too fast for me to keep up with it. But the program advocated by that party and by the government in office, that is the ultimate end to which it is leading. That is the reason the matter is raised.
It is a serious question of war or peace. It is not a question of accusations about positions or unilateral disarmament, whether or not they are advocated by anyone in this house. It is a matter of action by the minister and of the split personality that exists in the cabinet over this matter. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that it cannot be brushed aside or be pushed off into one corner by some-and I use this word in a general sense-scurrilous innuendos, without naming the people to whom they are directed.
As the parliamentary secretary indicated, the activity of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Harkness) was not improper. It is his responsibility as minister to speak his mind. But it is the statement that he made to promote in the armed services political activity, attempting to undo all the fine work in this matter by people like Dr. Schweitzer, Dr. Linus Pauling and others. I submit that this is the result of straight absolute confusion in the minds of the government about this matter. This is the effect of the statements of the Minister of National Defence.
I listened with interest to the comments of the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer). It is obvious that he still thinks he is associate minister of national defence in exhibiting that sort of schizophrenia for which the Liberal party is responsible. I have in my hand a document; I will be

gracious and call it by that name. It is entitled "The Record Speaks". It is published by the Conservative association of Canada, I presume.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Have you read it?

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Yes, I have read it.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: It is good is it not? There is nothing wrong with it.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: The hon. member says there is nothing wrong with it. It is full of falsehoods. I will relate them at another point.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: You are losing your sense of humour.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: When I look at my hon. friends my sense of humour picks up.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Order. The hon. member is taking off at a tangent, if I may say so. If he wishes to relate the document to the grievance, I suggest that he do it before he pursues it.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: I had fully intended to do so immediately but I was being pushed to one side by hon. members who remain in their seats. On page 14 of this document-I do not know whether it is a serial story or what it is-this particular piece of fiction, there are some quotations from the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) at the United Nations, September 26, 1960, a period of time to which my colleague, the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) referred. Like my friend the hon. member for Vancouver East I think they are excellent comments dealing with this self-same subject matter. I wish to quote from "The Record Speaks". You will notice, Mr. Speaker, that the colour has changed. It is getting to be a paler and paler blue all the time.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: You are getting deeper in the red.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
In the financial part it gets deeper in the red. As found at page 14, the Prime Minister said this:
I have frequently had occasion to urge publicly the end of nuclear weapons, the systematic control of missiles designed to deliver nuclear weapons of mass destruction,-
And so on.
Canada over and over again has advocated an end to nuclear testing.
He is another one who would ban the bomb, another one of those individuals whom the Minister of National Defence would like to send his charges off to quell. The country is full of people who believe explicitly in what the Prime Minister said. But the more that we get statements by the Minister of

Agriculture or rather, the Minister of National Defence-and I keep thinking of him as the Minister of Agriculture-it is obvious that he is going to make as much of a mess of this department also as he did of that one.
In any event, statements of this nature made by the Minister of National Defence, which by his silence must be accepted as factual, unless he now, in a belated way, wants to repudiate them and say he did not make them, will within this country undo all the good that has been done, as I said, by people like Dr. Schweitzer and Dr. Linus Pauling and the 2,000 scientists who signed the petition, and the work that has been advocated by the Prime Minister at the United Nations. It will also undo the work that has been done by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Green) on the disarmament question. All this work could well be unravelled, undone, emasculated and ruined by irresponsible statements of the nature of those attributed to the Minister of National Defence.
It is perhaps obvious that his long attachment with the Department of Agriculture got him in close association with what is decently referred to as fertilizer and which is now slopping over into defence policy.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: That is your level.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my remarks on this matter which has been brought up by the C.C.F. tonight is, as the minister has said, trying to make a mountain out of a grain of sand. It is just another illustration of the tactics they have carried on in this house.
No man and no government in this country is more interested in disarmament and the abolition of nuclear weapons than the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) and this government. But it is our duty to protect this country. We have never been known as an aggressive country. We are a country wishing to protect ourselves and the western hemisphere. It seems to me-and this is my own opinion and I have a right to that opinion- that that little corner down there would like to see our defences weakened by the abolition of nuclear weapons so that their big brothers from Russia could overrun this country.
I say that on these grounds, and I will quote a few remarks that I have here. Even the late Mr. Woodsworth, the first leader of the C.C.F. party, confessed on February 1, 1933, in the house of Commons:
It may well be that force may prove inevitable.
Then we go on to 1943, when the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) made that notable speech in Calgary. This has
National Defence
been recounted before, but I think it should go on record again. These are his words, as reported by the Calgary Herald:
Asked about the position of the police and military forces in the event of moves for a change, Mr. Winch said that when ''we become the government we will introduce socialism immediately," and would use the power of the police and the military forces to force those opposed to obey the law. "Those who defied the government's will would be treated as criminals," he declared, adding "If capitalism says no, then we know the answer- so did Russia".
These are the statements on which I am basing my opinion. There are one or two more. There is the statement made by Mr. Woodsworth on April 23, 1935:
"The socialist", Mr. Woodsworth says, "stands for the abolition of capitalism".

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I may be confused, but may I ask you whether the grievance is regarding a speech made by myself allegedly in 1943, or is it in reference to a speech made a couple of days ago by the Minister of National Defence?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. member who has the floor would indicate how he relates these matters to the point of grievance.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: I am just relating the reasons why they are bringing up this matter. They want us to give up nuclear weapons so that their big brothers in Russia can take over. I just have one more statement. This was reported in the Calgary Herald.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: If it is mine, I hope it is correct this time.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
Speaking to a C.C.F. rally of 1,000 people on April 23, 1935, Mr. Woodsworth made this clear and unequivocal declaration:
The doctrines of the C.C.F. are the doctrines of the united front or communist, and all that keeps us apart is a difference of tactics and a suspicion of insincerity.
That is why this matter has been brought up tonight. They do not want nuclear weapons in Canada for the simple reason that they want their big brothers in Russia to overrun this country, and we in this capitalist country do not want that.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am surprised how such a simple little grievance-

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Are your remarks on the same matter?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker. I am surprised how such a simple little grievance should raise such a storm of protest. It would seem to me that the minister in this case made a speech at H.M.C.S. Carleton. I think

National Defence
he admits that. I think he also admits that he stated a new policy as far as the reservists of Canada are concerned.
As an active military man over the years, with a good reputation, and getting into a department now that he should know something about-certainly more so than in the previous department-I am not surprised to find that he has asked his reservists to do something that he wishes to be done.
Reading the press statement we come to the conclusion that the reservists in Canada are going to be asked to help the minister in this way, "Let us get as big an appropriation out of my cabinet colleagues as possible and we will keep all you boys employed".
I do not blame the minister for this, if he wishes to do it and has the inclination. If he is, as the minister was, asked to make that statement, then he should make it. But I think the question now is not whether the C.C.F. is interested in banning the bomb, or whether we are neutralists, or what our position is going to be, but whether the minister agrees with the statements he is reported to have made at a meeting that he attended.
I think it is that simple. If this is a new policy of the Conservative party, then I think the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) should be told; I think the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Green) should be told, because we have three or four different policies going around. We in the opposition are entitled to know what the stand of the government is.
I do not believe we will ever find out what the Liberal stand is; we cannot follow them. If we are going to have airplanes, we can bird-watch; if we have no airplanes we cannot even do that. So I am not particularly concerned with what they stand for. I am concerned with the fact that the Canadian reservists should have an honest appraisal of what they are doing. If we are going to ask them to go out and spread our military strength, the fact that our country has a capable defence, then I think the minister should say so. He should be quite proud to say that that is his opinion and go on from that supposition.
If he was misquoted in this case; if he did not say that, he should say so. It is true that over the years reservists have been allowed much more freedom than the active army, the active air force or navy, who have been told they are not to participate in political action of any description except by special request, although allowance was made for certain people in the services to declare themselves political candidates during the period of war. With that exception they have 
not been able to do what the reservists have been able to do; but they are not acting in the line of duty.
If this is a change in policy-and it appears to us to be a change-then I think the minister should say so. But if he says this, I think he must go much further and make the statement that is requested by the opposition. He should give out information that is contrary to that being propagated by "ban the bomb" and other pacificist organizations. He should be in a position to give to the reservists more than just the speech that he gave off the cuff. He must come out with the new policy so that the reservists will have some opportunity at least of being informed, or half as well informed as the opposition.
The Prime Minister is giving leadership, the Secretary of State for External Affairs is giving leadership to those who say we should work toward disarmament and peace, toward banning the bomb. I think that at least the reservists should be given enough information so that they are not going to look silly putting forth a half-baked scheme that the minister may get up for his amusement for an after-dinner speech.
As I see it, that is all that is involved in this particular matter. If the minister has been misquoted, if he does not believe these things, then he should say so. If he does believe them he should have the gumption, in my opinion, to stand up and say, "I said them; I stand behind them, and if the other cabinet members do not like it they can go jump in the lake".

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened, along with everybody else, to the remarks of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Harkness) and, surprisingly enough, with my limited experience of only two and a half years in this house, I managed to understand fully the explanation provided when old-timers of the parliamentary scene do not seem to understand it or at least are not willing to understand it.
We are called upon at times to account to our constituents for the work being done in the House of Commons. I believe it would be very difficult to explain to those who elected us the hour and a half we spent tonight discussing this problem.
The government has to find answers to serious problems. Some important legislation is awaiting our consideration. And we are being asked now to spend an hour and a half to discuss a matter that the minister might have raised some place.

Mr. Speaker, for my part, I would rather consider, first of all, the military record of the Minister of National Defence and then his accomplishments both political and administrative. What he told us tonight in this house is worth a lot more than all those reports which were read to us and whose origin cannot even be ascertained.
I would rather stick to the tradition existing in this house and which gives a member claiming to have been misquoted, let us say, in the newspapers the opportunity to explain the situation and to have his word accepted by his colleagues.
The Minister of National Defence explained to us tonight what had taken place. I think we should all accept his word of honour. Second, he has witnessed and lived through the very events that he related.
Consequently, we are faced here with only hearsay such as the C.C.F. party like to spread. They preferred to rely on what they may have read.
The minister, who naturally was present on that occasion, told us exactly what had taken place, and I feel his word should be accepted. More especially as the position he holds is so closely connected with the one occupied by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Green) and both these gentlemen, let me emphasize it, have done a lot to bring about a well balanced and controlled disarmament.
At all events, I think this debate will have been a good thing since it will have indicated that our people-who are so much interested everywhere in the work done by the Minister of National Defence and the Secretary of State for External Affairs-can be very happy about the task performed by these two ministers.
I am not suggesting that this debate was begun in bad faith, I am only suggesting that it will nevertheless have been beneficial to the people.

Mr. Speaker, on this same grievance I will say only a few words. Indeed tonight's discussion should produce good results, I hope.
Not too long ago, the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) stated that the Conservative party failed to make its record known to the Canadian people. Ever since that statement was made, we have noted that ministers, took turns in delivering speeches here and there. Saturday's speech was one of the series; quite often however, those same ministers have had, not to retract, I would not say that, but they had to correct newspaper reports.
